strengths: Addresses a real and important limitation in class-pose decomposition methods: arbitrary canonical orientations produce inconsistent, shifted symmetry distributions.
The proposed canonical orientation normalization is simple, principled, and compatible with existing class-pose backbones such as IE-AEs.
The method is unsupervised and yields identity-centered distributions that are interpretable and comparable across classes.
The extension to 3D SO(3) symmetry discovery on molecular conformation data is a meaningful step beyond typical 2D benchmarks.
The paper includes detailed implementation and training hyperparameters, supporting reproducibility.
Qualitative visualizations demonstrate data-aligned canonicalization and the ability to distinguish partially symmetric classes such as 6 and 9.
The downstream OOD pose detection application illustrates practical utility of the learned symmetry distributions.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is incremental: estimating and subtracting/right-translating by an empirical Fréchet mean is a natural correction, and the main proposition relies on strong assumptions, including exact equivariance of the pose predictor ψ and negligible non-group noise.

The evaluation lacks comparisons to prior symmetry-discovery methods such as SGMs, Partial G-CNNs, VP G-CNNs, or WSCNNs on the same tasks; the main comparison is only against unnormalized IE-AE outputs.

The symmetries in the experiments are synthetically injected: MNIST/FashionMNIST rotations are drawn from known label-dependent distributions, and GEOM conformers are rotated by known matrix-Fisher distributions. This validates recovery of a controlled augmentation rather than discovery of unknown or approximate real-world symmetries.

The GEOM train/test split is performed per molecule, so test conformers come from molecule classes seen during training; there is no evaluation on unseen molecule classes or analysis of generalization of the learned Θ and Λ mappings.
The OOD pose detection application reports AUC scores without any baselines or ablations, making it difficult to assess the significance of the reported performance.
The k-NN approximation of the equivalence class is central to the method, but sensitivity to k and robustness to noisy invariant embeddings are only briefly examined and only on 2D data.

The Fréchet mean can be non-unique or ill-defined for uniform or multimodal distributions, which are precisely the challenging cases for symmetry discovery; the paper acknowledges this only partially.
There is no ablation comparing Fréchet-mean normalization against alternative centering choices such as mode, geodesic median, or robust M-estimators.
The 2D experiments may be relatively easy because the invariant encoder likely already clusters digits well, and no quantitative analysis of clustering/class-separation quality is provided.

strengths: Identifies a real issue in class-pose decomposition methods: arbitrary canonical orientations make relative pose distributions inconsistent and hard to compare.
Proposes a simple, principled normalization based on the Fréchet mean, yielding identity-centered, interpretable symmetry descriptors and data-aligned canonicals.
Provides a theoretical proposition linking the observed relative-pose distribution to the true symmetry distribution under noise and exact equivariance assumptions.
Demonstrates qualitative benefits on 2D images, including handling of partial symmetries such as digits 6 and 9, and shows an extension to SO(3) molecular conformations.
Includes a practical downstream application: out-of-distribution pose detection, which illustrates the usefulness of the recovered distributions.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is essentially post-hoc centering of relative pose distributions via the empirical Fréchet mean, a standard geometric operation.

The evaluation is largely synthetic: rotations are artificially injected using known distributions, so the method recovers augmentation distributions rather than discovering intrinsic symmetries. The 3D GEOM experiment applies synthetic matrix-Fisher rotations, making the “real-world 3D symmetry discovery” claim overstated.
No convincing baselines: the paper does not quantitatively compare against SGM, IE-AE without normalization, Partial G-CNNs, VP G-CNNs, Augerino, or other symmetry-learning methods on the same tasks.

The theory relies on strong assumptions—exact equivariance of ψ, small bounded noise, compact domain, unique/Lipschitz Fréchet mean, and no learning error—that are not verified in practice. The kNN class approximation is also not theoretically justified.
The inference procedure assumes known parametric forms (e.g., matrix-Fisher) for symmetry distributions, limiting generality and contradicting the paper’s framing of flexible symmetry discovery.

Class discovery via connected components / kNN in the invariant latent space is heuristic and may fail in complex data; there is little analysis of class separation, neighborhood-size sensitivity, or failure cases.
Reproducibility is weakened by the hidden code link and the lack of strong quantitative results; several experimental details are deferred to the appendix, and no external baselines are provided.
Claims about “first demonstrations in 3D” and “paving the way” are not sufficiently supported by rigorous experiments or high-impact evidence.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: unsupervised discovery of instance-specific symmetry distributions from unlabeled data, and identifies the overlooked issue of arbitrary canonical poses in class-pose decomposition methods.

The proposed canonical orientation normalization is simple, intuitive, and well-motivated, using the Fréchet mean to align relative transformations into identity-centered, comparable symmetry descriptors.

Provides a theoretical result (Proposition 3.1) showing that the empirical distribution of normalized pose transformations approximates the target symmetry distribution under stated assumptions, giving the method some formal grounding.
Extends beyond typical 2D symmetry-discovery benchmarks to SO(3) on the large-scale GEOM molecular dataset, demonstrating scalability and the ability to recover 3D rotation distributions.
Demonstrates practical application benefits, especially improved canonicalization and out-of-distribution pose detection, with qualitative and quantitative results on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and GEOM.
The paper is generally clear, well-structured, and includes extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, and a code link, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evaluation largely tests recovery of injected/known transformations rather than discovery of naturally occurring symmetries: MNIST/FashionMNIST rotations and GEOM matrix-Fisher rotations are artificially imposed by the experimenters, and the method estimates the assumed parametric family, so it is not fully demonstrating unsupervised discovery of unknown intrinsic symmetry distributions.

There are no quantitative comparisons to prior symmetry-discovery or partial-equivariance methods such as SGM, VP G-CNNs, Augerino, Partial G-CNNs, WSCNNs, or related unsupervised symmetry-learning approaches; comparisons are mainly qualitative or ablations against unnormalized IE-AE.

The 3D GEOM evaluation claims real-world symmetry discovery, but the true symmetry distributions are synthetic and injected after aligning molecular conformers, which may overstate real-world validity and does not test approximate or naturally occurring molecular orientation distributions.

The method relies on a known or assumed parametric form for the symmetry distribution (e.g., uniform, Gaussian, matrix-Fisher) when training the Θ predictor; real unsupervised discovery would likely involve unknown or misspecified distribution families, which is not evaluated.

The class approximation via k-nearest neighbors or connected components in the invariant space is central, but sensitivity to the equivalence threshold, choice of k, imperfect clustering, and noisy non-group variations is only lightly explored; failure modes when the invariant space does not separate classes are not analyzed.

The theoretical proposition relies on strong assumptions: exact group equivariance, small bounded noise, Fréchet mean uniqueness/convexity conditions, and continuous ψ. These may not hold for real data with partial, approximate, or multimodal symmetries, and the Fréchet mean as a 'natural pose' can be non-intuitive for multimodal distributions.
The out-of-distribution pose detection results are moderate (AUC 0.75 on GEOM) and lack baselines or deeper analysis of thresholds, calibration, and practical failure cases.
Some notational and proof presentation issues remain in the appendix, and the proposition's handling of general Lie groups and Fréchet mean equivariance could be made more rigorous.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: arbitrary canonical orientations in class-pose decomposition methods, which distort symmetry discovery and downstream performance.
Proposes a simple, architecture-agnostic post-hoc correction (RECON) via Fréchet mean normalization, supported by Proposition 3.1 and an extension with Tukey-Fréchet robust estimation.
Enables unsupervised discovery of instance-specific symmetry distributions and provides useful applications: OOD pose detection and test-time canonicalization for frozen pretrained models.
Demonstrates strong practical gains in test-time canonicalization, e.g., improving rotated MNIST accuracy from 66.90% to 92.94% without retraining the backbone.
Extends symmetry discovery experiments to 3D molecular conformations (GEOM-QM9), which is a nontrivial and valuable step beyond typical 2D settings.
Provides detailed implementation and reproducibility information, including model architectures, hyperparameters, and training procedures.
Shows interpretable natural canonicalizations and ability to handle partial symmetries such as distinguishing rotated 6 and 9, unlike standard equivariant methods.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are limited: experiments mainly compare against the IE-AE backbone, with no quantitative comparison to SGM or other symmetry discovery methods such as VP G-CNNs, WSCNNs, Partial G-CNNs, or Augerino.
Test-time canonicalization lacks simple baselines such as PCA/moment-based alignment or test-time augmentation, making the practical advantages less clear.
Evaluation relies heavily on synthetic rotations/augmentations with known ground-truth transformation distributions rather than naturally occurring symmetry distributions in images or molecules.

The proposed robust Tukey-Fréchet estimator is not used in the main experiments; experiments rely on classical Fréchet mean or matrix-Fisher mode, so the robustness benefits are only shown in simulations.
The OOD detection section references a numeric AUC-ROC table (Table 5) that is not present in the main manuscript, weakening the quantitative support for that claim.
The method depends on a class-pose backbone and a predefined group, and does not discover group structure itself; it inherits limitations of the backbone and the k-NN/equivalence-class heuristic.

Theoretical guarantees assume idealized continuity, small noise, and consistency of the empirical Fréchet mean; finite-sample behavior and sensitivity to pseudo-label noise are not rigorously characterized.

The claim of being the first to extend symmetry discovery to 3D groups may be somewhat overstated given the controlled augmentation setting, and broader positioning against existing 3D equivariance/symmetry work could be strengthened.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and under-addressed issue in class-pose decomposition methods: arbitrary canonical orientations cause shifted relative-pose distributions and out-of-distribution canonicalizations.
The proposed RECON normalization is simple, architecture-agnostic, and easy to apply post hoc to a trained class-pose backbone.
The theoretical proposition gives a plausible justification for using the empirical Fréchet mean of relative poses as a canonical offset estimator under idealized assumptions.
The extension to 3D SO(3) and the GEOM-QM9 experiments are a useful step beyond typical 2D-only symmetry-discovery evaluations.
The downstream applications—OOD pose detection and inference-time canonicalization for frozen backbones—are practical and relevant if validated more strongly.
The paper provides substantial implementation details, including architectures, hyperparameters, and reproducibility practices.
weaknesses: The core contribution is incremental: centering the relative-pose distribution by subtracting/right-multiplying the Fréchet mean is a natural post-processing step. The main proposition essentially formalizes that if the canonical offset is constant per class, the Fréchet mean estimates it.

The evaluation does not convincingly demonstrate unsupervised discovery of unknown, instance-specific symmetries. The “ground-truth” symmetries in all main experiments are injected by the authors via controlled rotations, so the method is evaluated on recovery of known synthetic augmentations rather than natural symmetries in real data.

Baselines are too weak. The paper mostly compares against IE-AE, while the closest related method, SGM (Allingham et al., 2024), is discussed but not quantitatively compared for symmetry distribution recovery or downstream tasks. Other relevant baselines such as test-time augmentation, frame averaging, canonicalization methods, or retrained equivariant models are missing.

The test-time canonicalization baseline “IE-AE canonicalization” is arbitrary and collapses to near-chance accuracy, making it trivial for RECON to outperform. This does not establish competitiveness with existing practical invariance mechanisms.

The method depends heavily on the underlying IE-AE backbone and on kNN-based class approximation in the invariant latent space. Sensitivity to k is only briefly explored, and equivalence-class quality is not systematically validated on the image benchmarks.

The theoretical assumptions are strong and not verified in practice: ψ is assumed to be G-equivariant, the canonical offset is assumed constant per class, noise is assumed very small, and the target distribution is assumed to be Fréchet-centered at identity. Finite-sample and model-mismatch errors are not analyzed.

The robust Tukey-Fréchet extension is heuristic and introduces a threshold parameter c with little theoretical guidance. It is presented as a drop-in replacement but is not rigorously justified for the claimed consistency.

The claims are stronger than the evidence: “unsupervised discovery of instance-specific symmetry distributions” and “first time” 3D symmetry discovery are not fully supported by controlled augmentation experiments, and the method is not shown to work in natural multi-object or in-the-wild settings.

OOD detection and symmetry recovery results lack statistical testing, confidence intervals, or error bars in the main text. The reported comparisons are not sufficient to judge robustness across datasets, backbones, or hyperparameters.
The paper acknowledges dataset-bias concerns but does not analyze how canonicalization choices or latent clustering could perpetuate or amplify biases in real-world data.

strengths: Addresses a real and under-explored issue: arbitrary canonical orientation in class-pose decomposition, which can make learned symmetry distributions inconsistent and out-of-distribution.

Provides a clean and intuitive normalization: right-multiply relative poses by the inverse Fréchet mean; Proposition 3.1 links this to recovery of identity-centered symmetry distributions, with proof in appendix.
Extends symmetry discovery beyond 2D to SO(3) on GEOM-QM9, with reasonable quantitative evaluation using matrix-Fisher parameter error and downstream applications.
Demonstrates practical value via OOD pose detection and test-time canonicalization, improving frozen pre-trained classifiers without retraining (e.g., MNIST 66.9→92.9, F-MNIST 57.5→80.3).
Reproducibility is strong: detailed appendix on architectures, training, pseudo-label computation, and code promised.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is limited to rotations and synthetically imposed symmetry distributions; it is not clear how well the method discovers natural, instance-specific symmetries in less controlled data.

Missing direct quantitative comparison to closely related symmetry-discovery baselines such as SGM, WSCNN, VP G-CNNs, or partial G-CNNs; IE-AE is the main baseline, but SGM is discussed as most related and only compared qualitatively.

The method depends on several practical heuristics (e.g., k-NN class approximation with k=25, choice of Fréchet/Tukey-Fréchet estimator, parametric matrix-Fisher assumption) whose sensitivity and failure modes are not fully characterized.

The theoretical claim assumes ψ is continuous on a compact domain and that noise ε' is small; these assumptions may not hold for real-world data or deep networks, and the bound is asymptotic rather than finite-sample.
The main experiments use SO(2)/SO(3) rotations; broader groups (e.g., SE(3), scaling, non-Euclidean symmetries) and object-centric settings are left to future work, limiting current scope.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a real weakness in class-pose decomposition methods: arbitrary canonical orientations induce shifted, non-identity-centered pose distributions and OOD canonicalizations. The proposed Fréchet-mean normalization is simple, intuitive, and theoretically motivated.

Proposition 3.1 provides a convergence argument showing that right-translating empirical relative poses by their Fréchet mean approximates the identity-centered target distribution under stated assumptions. The Tukey-Fréchet extension is also a sensible robustification for multimodal distributions.
The method enables unsupervised instance-level symmetry discovery, OOD pose detection, and a plug-and-play test-time canonicalization layer that does not require retraining the downstream model.

The empirical evaluation spans both 2D images and large-scale 3D molecular conformations, with results showing consistent improvements over IE-AE and competitive performance against EquiAdapt in several test-time canonicalization settings.
The paper is generally well-written, includes detailed appendices, code, and implementation details, and the computational overhead of test-time canonicalization is shown to be small.
weaknesses: The core contribution is relatively incremental: it mainly adds a post-hoc right-translation/normalization step on top of existing class-pose decomposition backbones such as IE-AE. It does not solve the harder problem of discovering the group G itself, and its effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of the pretrained backbone.

There is a mismatch between theory and practice: Proposition 3.1 relies on the classical Fréchet mean under strong assumptions, while the main experiments use circular means for SO(2) and matrix-Fisher modes for SO(3). The proposed Tukey-Fréchet robust estimator is motivated and simulated but not systematically evaluated on the main benchmarks, leaving multimodal and stabilizer-ambiguity cases under-validated.

The evaluation lacks direct quantitative comparisons to closely related instance-level symmetry distribution methods such as SGM, Implicit-PDF, LieGAN, or LaLiGAN, even though SGM is explicitly identified as the most related prior work. This makes it difficult to assess the relative advantage of RECON beyond the IE-AE baseline.

Class equivalence is defined heuristically via k-NN connectivity in the invariant latent space. Although the authors analyze hit rates, this assumption can fail when latent classes overlap, as acknowledged for FashionMNIST, and performance is sensitive to the neighborhood size k.

The downstream gains in the 3D GEOM-QM9 experiment are modest (e.g., 52.40% to 55.92%) and remain far below specialized equivariant SEGNN performance (98.55%), limiting the practical significance of test-time canonicalization in complex 3D settings.

Some claims seem stronger than the evidence, and certain comparisons are not fully convincing. For example, the description of EquiAdapt as label-supervised is potentially misleading for its zero-shot canonicalization setup, and table/column formatting inconsistencies make the main results harder to verify.

The method is demonstrated mostly on controlled rotations with known SO(2)/SO(3) groups and relatively simple or synthetic augmentations; broader applicability to natural images, multi-object scenes, unknown groups, and object-centric symmetries remains largely a future direction.

strengths: Identifies a real practical issue in class-pose decomposition methods: arbitrary canonical orientations induce shifted, non-identifiable relative pose distributions and OOD canonicalizations.
The proposed correction is simple and architecture-agnostic: estimate the Fréchet mean of relative poses for a class and right-translate by its inverse to obtain identity-centered pose distributions.

Provides a theoretical argument (Proposition 3.1) showing that under the class-pose model, the empirical normalized distribution approximates the target distribution as noise vanishes and sample size grows.
Demonstrates a useful plug-in application: unsupervised test-time canonicalization can improve frozen pretrained models without retraining, with gains on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and GEOM-QM9.
Includes practical details, hyperparameters, and code release, and the paper is generally well written and clear.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the core operation is essentially centering relative pose distributions by their Fréchet mean. Proposition 3.1 is a fairly direct consequence of equivariance / isometry equivariance of the Fréchet mean, not a deep theoretical advance.

The paper claims unsupervised symmetry discovery, but it does not actually discover the group or unknown symmetries. It assumes a known group G and relies on an existing class-pose backbone with an (approximately) equivariant pose predictor ψ, so the contribution is more narrowly canonical orientation normalization.

Evaluation is mostly on synthetic injected rotations: rotated MNIST/FashionMNIST and QM9 conformers with controlled matrix-Fisher SO(3) rotations. There is little evidence on real unknown, naturally occurring instance-specific symmetries with reliable ground truth.

The key hyperparameter k for the kNN-based class approximation is selected using ground-truth symmetry parameters in Appendix D.2, which violates the unsupervised premise. Fixed-kNN approximation is also not covered by the consistency proof, which assumes samples from the full class.

The robust Tukey-Fréchet extension is introduced and motivated as an important contribution, but it is not used or validated in the main experiments; the experiments use standard Fréchet/circular mean/mode instead. The title and claims overstate robustness relative to the empirical support.

Baselines and comparisons are incomplete. SGM, the most related instance-level symmetry distribution method, is only qualitatively discussed in Figure 2 and not quantitatively compared. Other symmetry discovery methods are also not evaluated for distribution recovery.

The method relies on strong assumptions: the invariant latent space must separate classes, pose predictions must be equivariant, and the group action is global over the whole input. These fail in many realistic object-centric or natural-image settings, as the authors acknowledge, but no practical solution is provided.

The class equivalence definition and its approximation via kNN remain ad hoc, and the paper shows failure modes (e.g., FashionMNIST class overlap) without fully addressing them. Ablations on the robust estimator and the class construction are insufficient.

strengths: Addresses a clear and relevant problem: arbitrary canonical orientations in class-pose decomposition methods lead to shifted, non-interpretable pose distributions.
Proposes a simple and intuitive normalization: right-translation by the empirical Fréchet mean of predicted relative poses, with a theoretical consistency result (Proposition 3.1).
Demonstrates broad empirical validation on 2D image datasets and a large-scale 3D molecular dataset (GEOM-QM9), going beyond typical 2D-only symmetry discovery work.
Provides practical downstream applications: unsupervised OOD pose detection and a plug-and-play, retraining-free test-time canonicalization layer for frozen pre-trained models.
Good reproducibility: code is publicly available, implementation details are extensive, and appendices include hyperparameters, runtime analysis, and additional experiments.
The method is architecture-agnostic in principle and can be attached to existing class-pose backbones, which lowers adoption barriers.
Qualitative and quantitative results on MNIST/FashionMNIST and GEOM-QM9 convincingly show recovery of per-class rotation distributions and improved downstream classification in several settings.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively simple and incremental: estimating a Fréchet mean per class and applying a right translation. The novelty may be limited relative to prior class-pose decomposition work.

The method relies heavily on the quality of the underlying IE-AE backbone and on kNN clustering in the invariant latent space. This is fragile for natural images and inter-class latent overlap, as the authors themselves acknowledge, and the proposed fixes are not fully evaluated.

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic rotations on MNIST/FashionMNIST and one molecular dataset, with only SO(2)/SO(3) rotation groups. There is no real-world natural-image benchmark or non-rotation group.

For symmetry discovery, quantitative comparisons are mostly against IE-AE; other relevant symmetry-discovery methods (e.g., SGM, LieGAN, VP G-CNNs, WSCNNs) are discussed but not quantitatively compared. SGM is only qualitatively compared.

The test-time canonicalization comparison with EquiAdapt is potentially confounded by different supervision/training setups, and some table formatting is confusing, making it harder to verify the exact fairness of comparisons.

The theoretical result assumes continuity of ψ on a compact domain, small noise ε′→0, and favorable Fréchet mean properties (e.g., strict convexity/Lipschitz behavior). These assumptions may not hold for learned networks in practice.

The definition of the 'natural' pose as the Fréchet mean can be ambiguous for multimodal or highly symmetric objects and may reflect dataset bias rather than semantic orientation. The proposed Tukey–Fréchet extension is not integrated into the main experiments.

The claim that centering improves OOD detection is somewhat at odds with the theoretical reference-frame invariance result; the observed gains are attributed to optimization but are not deeply analyzed.

Ablations are helpful but still limited: sensitivity to k is explored, but other design choices (e.g., loss weighting, parametric distribution assumptions, choice of robust estimator) are not systematically ablated.
